title: A Thousand Is More Than Four: The Quiet Power of Teaching
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Reflecting the day after a presidential election, Stuart defends his deliberately nonpartisan stance on the blog while arguing that teaching itself is nonetheless inescapably political -- not in a partisan sense, but because it empowers and emancipates students to engage with reality in new ways. He traces this realization back to early pushback he received while writing about the Common Core, when a reviewer argued that his apolitical stance was itself a political choice. He illustrates the point with a ninth-grade student's reflection on finally being able to follow and understand election coverage after a sequence of current-events readings, vocabulary instruction, and writing prompts. Stuart closes by arguing that the deepest, most durable political act available to him is simply teaching his students well -- modeling civility, kindness, and neighbor-love -- because its effects outlast any single election cycle.
points: Stuart reframes "apolitical teaching" not as neutrality but as a specific political stance: teaching is inherently political because it empowers and emancipates students' capacity to engage with reality.

He traces his own view's evolution from resisting to accepting a reviewer's critique of his early Common Core writing, modeling intellectual growth in response to disagreement rather than defensiveness.

The student example (a ninth grader newly able to follow election coverage) is offered as concrete evidence of how a specific instructional sequence -- articles, vocabulary, writing -- changes a student's actual relationship to reality.

His closing claim -- that teaching's ripple effects "will reverberate for a thousand years" -- reframes the significance of daily classroom work against the comparatively short half-life of electoral politics.
quotes: But there were some during that period who argued my apolitical stance was misguided. Teaching, one reviewer argued, is an inherently political act; not taking a stand is taking one.

Teaching is political, in that it empowers and emancipates the learner to experience and interact with reality in ways that, previously, they could not. I do take a stand, which is that I'm a teacher and so I'll teach.
Some takeaways that I have from the presidential election is that it's weird that I can finally pay more attention to things that are going on around me and understand the election.

Rather, the greatest good I can do with my working life — for my students, my country, my world — is 1) to help my students master the disciplines I am tasked with teaching them and 2) to help you help yours do the same.
A good education has an impact that humans fail to measure adequately. Its true effects are seen not in academic calendar years or on standardized tests but rather in generations and on cultures.
The ripples you and I are making as we enlist our hearts and minds in the mundane-seeming work we do will reverberate for a thousand years.
